concept: Purpose and definition of the chandelle
q: What is a chandelle and what is it meant to show the examiner?
a: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180 degree climbing turn, begun from approximately straight-and-level flight and finished wings level in a nose-high attitude just above stall speed. It is graded on planning, smoothness and coordination rather than on how much altitude I gain, and it shows I can manage a large, continuous change of pitch, bank and airspeed while holding the airplane right at the edge of its climb performance. The ACS task is CA.V.C.

concept: What the chandelle demonstrates - why a commercial maneuver
q: Why is the chandelle on the commercial certificate rather than the private?
a: Because it demands precise, planned control of the airplane through its full speed range in one continuous maneuver. The chandelle shows coordination as the airspeed decays and the left-turning tendencies grow, shows I can divide attention between attitude, airspeed and a ground reference, and shows I can arrive at a planned point with the airplane at a planned energy state. The standard asks for maximum performance, meaning the most altitude gained for the 180 degrees of turn with the airplane still under full control.

concept: Clearing the area and pre-maneuver checks before a chandelle
q: What do you do in the Warrior before you start a chandelle?
a: Clearing turns and a scan for traffic first; then a pre-maneuver flow: fuel on the fullest tank, electric fuel pump on, mixture rich, engine gauges green, seat belts and loose items secured, and carburetor heat checked. I confirm I am high enough that the maneuver finishes no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, pick a prominent reference off the wingtip, and set up with the wind perpendicular to the entry heading.

concept: Entry configuration and entry airspeed for the chandelle, Warrior II specific
q: What airspeed and configuration do you enter a chandelle at in the Warrior?
a: Clean, flaps up, and at or below maneuvering speed. For the 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II the POH Section 2 gives design maneuvering speed as 111 KIAS at 2,440 lb, falling to 88 KIAS at 1,531 lb, so I enter at or just below that figure for my weight. The ACS wording is to establish the manufacturer's recommended entry airspeed, or if none is published, no more than maneuvering speed. The airplane is trimmed and in balanced, level flight at the entry.

concept: Why maneuvering speed is the ceiling for the entry speed
q: Why must the chandelle entry speed not exceed maneuvering speed?
a: Because the chandelle begins with an abrupt, large pitch input and the airplane must be slow enough that it stalls before it can be overstressed. The Warrior II POH Section 2 says do not make full or abrupt control movements above 111 KIAS at 2,440 lb, and it cautions that maneuvering speed decreases at lighter weight, so I interpolate down toward the 88 KIAS figure given for 1,531 lb rather than using the gross weight number at light weight.

concept: Minimum altitude for the chandelle - 1,500 feet AGL
q: What is the minimum altitude for a chandelle and why that number?
a: The ACS requires an altitude that allows the maneuver to be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. The chandelle finishes just above stall speed with a high nose and low energy, so the number exists to leave room for a stall recovery or an inadvertent spin entry with altitude to spare. In practice I enter well above that because the chandelle is a climbing maneuver, so the finish is higher than the entry.

concept: ACS task code for the chandelle
q: Which ACS task is the chandelle and in which area of operation?
a: It is Task C in Area of Operation V, Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers, of the Commercial Pilot Airman Certification Standards FAA-S-ACS-7B; the task code is CA.V.C. The neighboring tasks in the same area are steep turns CA.V.A, steep spiral CA.V.B, lazy eight CA.V.D and eights on pylons CA.V.E.

concept: ACS tolerance - bank angle approximately 30 degrees
q: What bank angle does the ACS call for in a chandelle?
a: Approximately 30 degrees of bank, established at the entry and held constant through the first 90 degrees of turn. The ACS says approximately rather than giving a plus-or-minus band, but a bank much shallower than 30 degrees makes the airplane take too long to turn 180 degrees and it runs out of airspeed early, while much steeper costs climb performance because more of the lift is turning the airplane instead of lifting it.

concept: ACS tolerance - rollout complete at the 180 degree point, heading plus or minus 10 degrees
q: What heading tolerance applies to the chandelle?
a: The rollout must be complete at the 180 degree point, plus or minus 10 degrees of the reciprocal of the entry heading. That is the only plus-or-minus number in the whole task: the wings come level exactly as the airplane passes through the heading opposite the one it entered on, not before and not after.

concept: ACS tolerance - the only numeric tolerance in the chandelle task
q: Is there an altitude or airspeed tolerance on a chandelle?
a: No. The chandelle has no altitude tolerance and no airspeed tolerance; the only plus-or-minus figure in the task is the plus or minus 10 degrees on the heading at the 180 degree point. The other standards are qualitative or limiting: approximately 30 degrees of bank, finish just above stall speed without stalling, and complete the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.

concept: ACS tolerance - finish just above stall speed, momentarily avoiding a stall
q: What should the airspeed be as the chandelle finishes?
a: Just above stall speed, with the airplane held momentarily at that airspeed and not allowed to stall. The ACS wording is to complete the rollout at the 180 degree point just above a stall airspeed and maintain that airspeed momentarily while avoiding a stall. A stall warning chirp at the top is acceptable; an actual break is a failure of the task, and finishing with a comfortable margin of extra speed means the maneuver was not flown at maximum performance.

concept: ACS element - resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude
q: What does the ACS want after the 180 degree point of a chandelle?
a: Resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude. I lower the nose smoothly to the level attitude and let the airspeed build back to cruise while keeping the altitude I earned; dumping the nose and diving away throws away the altitude the maneuver just gained and is a common way to spoil an otherwise good chandelle.

concept: Stage A - the entry: establishing bank, then pitch and power together
q: Walk me through the entry to a chandelle.
a: From level flight at or below maneuvering speed, I roll smoothly to approximately 30 degrees of bank in the direction of the turn, then simultaneously begin increasing pitch and apply the power the airplane will use for the whole maneuver, keeping it coordinated. The bank is set first and then held; the pitch is increased progressively, not snatched, so the airspeed bleeds off smoothly over the first 90 degrees of turn.

concept: Stage A to B - entry to the 90 degree point
q: What should the airplane be doing between the entry and the 90 degree point?
a: Constant bank of approximately 30 degrees, steadily increasing pitch, steadily decreasing airspeed, and a continuous climb. The bank does not change at all during this half; only the pitch changes. The airplane reaches its highest pitch attitude at the 90 degree point, and from there the pitch is frozen while the bank starts coming out.

concept: Stage B - what happens at the 90 degree point
q: What is the 90 degree point of a chandelle and what changes there?
a: It is the halfway point of the turn and the hinge of the maneuver: the pitch attitude has reached its maximum and stops increasing, and I begin a coordinated constant rate rollout that will be finished exactly at the 180 degree point. Power stays where it was set. Nothing about the pitch changes from here on; the only thing changing is the bank coming out at a steady rate and the airspeed continuing to decay.

concept: Stage B to C - the 90 degree point to the 180 degree point
q: How do you fly the second half of a chandelle?
a: Hold the pitch attitude established at the 90 degree point absolutely constant, hold the power, and roll out at a constant rate so the wings come level exactly as the airplane reaches the reciprocal heading. As the bank reduces, the vertical component of lift increases and the climb steepens while the airspeed keeps decaying; that combination is what makes the pitch feel like it wants to drop and is why holding it takes increasing back pressure and increasing right rudder.

concept: Stage C - completion of the chandelle
q: Describe the completion of the chandelle.
a: At the 180 degree point the wings are level, the heading is the reciprocal of the entry heading within plus or minus 10 degrees, and the airplane is just above stall speed with the nose high. I hold that attitude and airspeed momentarily without stalling, then lower the nose gently to level flight and accelerate back to cruise with as little loss of altitude as possible, and reset power and trim.

concept: Where the altitude gain is largest during the chandelle
q: Does the airplane climb more in the first half or the second half of a chandelle?
a: It climbs throughout, but the rate of climb is greatest in the second 90 degrees, because as the bank is rolled out the vertical component of lift increases and more of the airplane's energy goes into climbing instead of turning. The first half is where the pitch is being built and the airspeed traded away; the second half is where that traded energy shows up as altitude.

concept: Reference selection - identifying the 90 and 180 degree points
q: How do you know where the 90 and 180 degree points are in a chandelle?
a: By picking a prominent ground reference off the wingtip before entry: a road, a section line or a lake edge lying 90 degrees to the entry heading. The reference is abeam at the start, and the airplane is pointed at it, or has it directly off the nose, at the 90 degree point. The heading indicator backs it up for the 180 degree point, but the maneuver is flown by looking outside, with the instruments only cross-checked.

concept: Setting up with the wind perpendicular to the entry heading
q: Which way do you line up relative to the wind before a chandelle?
a: With the wind perpendicular to the entry heading, so the airplane turns into the wind. The chandelle has no ground-track requirement, but turning into the wind keeps the airplane from drifting away from the practice area during the slow, low-groundspeed part of the maneuver, and it keeps the chosen 90 degree reference in roughly the same place instead of sliding downwind.

concept: Power setting for the chandelle in a 160 hp fixed-pitch Warrior
q: What do you do with the throttle during a chandelle in the Warrior?
a: Apply full power as the pitch starts up and leave it there for the whole maneuver. The Warrior II has a fixed-pitch propeller and a 160 horsepower Lycoming O-320, so there is no propeller control to set and no manifold pressure to manage: the throttle goes forward once, at the entry, and the mixture stays rich at these altitudes. Power is not changed at the 90 degree point and is only reduced after the maneuver is complete.

concept: Right rudder requirement as airspeed decays
q: Why does the chandelle need more and more right rudder as it goes on?
a: Because the left-turning tendencies grow as the airspeed falls with full power applied. P-factor increases as the angle of attack increases, the descending blade on the right produces more thrust, and slipstream, torque and gyroscopic effects all add left yaw; the rudder's effectiveness falls at the same time because the airflow over it is slowing. The result is that right rudder pressure must increase continuously all the way to the 180 degree point, and more of it is needed in a left chandelle than a right one.

concept: Recovery if the airplane stalls or buffets during the chandelle
q: The stall warning is blaring and you feel buffet at the 170 degree point. What do you do?
a: Relax back pressure immediately to reduce the angle of attack, keep the wings coming level with coordinated aileron and rudder, and keep the power in; once flying, level off and accept that the chandelle was flown with too much pitch. The one thing I will not do is pick up a dropping wing with aileron alone at that angle of attack, because the yaw from an uncoordinated recovery is how a stall becomes a spin. The 1,500 feet AGL floor exists for exactly this moment.

concept: Common error - initial bank too steep or too shallow
q: What goes wrong in a chandelle if the initial bank is wrong?
a: Too shallow and the airplane will not have turned 180 degrees by the time the airspeed decays, so I either stall before the rollout or have to steepen late and ruin the constant-bank requirement. Too steep and the turn finishes early with too much airspeed left and far less altitude gained, because lift is being spent on turning instead of climbing. The target is approximately 30 degrees, set before the pitch starts up.

concept: Common error - allowing the bank to change during the first 90 degrees
q: Why is a varying bank angle in the first half of a chandelle an error?
a: Because the first 90 degrees is defined by a constant bank with only the pitch changing. If the bank wanders, the turn rate wanders with it, so the airplane does not arrive at the 90 degree point with the pitch and airspeed it should have, and the constant-rate rollout in the second half will not finish on the reciprocal heading. The usual cause is letting the overbanking tendency go uncorrected as the airplane slows.

concept: Common error - pitch not increasing continuously in the first half
q: What happens if you set a pitch attitude at the entry and hold it to the 90 degree point?
a: The maneuver becomes a shallow climbing turn rather than a chandelle, and the airplane arrives at the 180 degree point with far too much airspeed and too little altitude. The first 90 degrees requires a continuously increasing pitch attitude, reaching its maximum exactly at the 90 degree point; the airspeed should be falling steadily the entire time, not sitting on one number.

concept: Common error - excessive pitch rate, stalling before the 180
q: What is the consequence of raising the nose too quickly in a chandelle?
a: The airspeed decays before the turn is finished, so I reach the stall somewhere short of the 180 degree point and either stall the airplane or have to lower the nose and ruin the constant pitch attitude. The pitch must be fed in gradually so the airspeed arrives just above stall speed exactly at the 180 degree point, not sooner. Rushing the pitch is the most common cause of a failed chandelle.

concept: Common error - not holding a constant pitch attitude in the second half
q: What is wrong with letting the nose drop between the 90 and 180 degree points?
a: It defeats the maneuver. The second 90 degrees requires a constant pitch attitude while the bank comes out; if the nose sags, the airplane stops trading airspeed for altitude, arrives at the 180 with too much speed and too little altitude, and the examiner sees a steep turn rather than a chandelle. The nose sags because the back pressure required keeps increasing as the airspeed falls and the bank reduces.

concept: Common error - rollout rate not constant, or rollout not complete at the 180
q: What is the error if you are still banked passing the reciprocal heading?
a: The rollout rate was not constant, usually because it was started late or flown in steps rather than continuously. The requirement is a coordinated constant rate rollout begun at the 90 degree point and completed precisely at the 180 degree point; rolling out early leaves the airplane level and still turning short of the heading, and rolling out late blows through the plus or minus 10 degree heading tolerance.

concept: Common error - uncoordinated flight, insufficient right rudder
q: What does the ball do in a badly flown chandelle and why does it matter?
a: It slides to the right of center as the airplane slows at full power, because the pilot is not feeding in the increasing right rudder the left-turning tendencies demand. That skid costs climb performance, makes the maneuver untidy, and at an airspeed just above the stall it is the setup for a spin, since a skidding stall drops the inside wing. Coordination is a graded element in the task, not a nicety.

concept: Common error - finishing with excess airspeed or stalling the airplane
q: Is a chandelle that finishes 15 knots above stall speed acceptable?
a: It is safe but it is not the maneuver: the task asks for the airplane to finish just above stall speed and to hold that momentarily. Finishing fast means the pitch was too low or the rollout was flown early, so the airplane was never operating at maximum performance. The opposite error, an actual stall break at the top, is a disqualifying loss of control, so the target is the narrow band just above the stall with the warning horn just beginning.

concept: Common error - losing altitude after the maneuver is complete
q: The chandelle is done and the airplane sinks 200 feet. What went wrong?
a: The nose was lowered too far or too fast while the airplane was still slow, so it accelerated by descending. The ACS element is to resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude: lower the nose only to the level attitude, hold that attitude, and let the airspeed build with power still applied, then reduce power and trim once at cruise speed.

concept: Common error - failing to clear the area or using a poor reference
q: What are the two setup errors an examiner will catch before a chandelle even starts?
a: Not clearing the area with proper clearing turns and a traffic scan, and picking a vague ground reference that cannot be seen once the nose comes up. The whole maneuver is flown by outside reference, so the 90 degree point needs to be something unmistakable such as a road or a shoreline; and because the airplane ends up slow and high-pitched with a long nose-high blind spot, the clearing turns are a graded part of the task, not a formality.

concept: Purpose and definition of the lazy eight
q: What is a lazy eight?
a: It is two 180 degree climbing and descending turns flown in opposite directions, with the nose tracing a symmetrical figure eight on its side against the horizon. Every control pressure, the pitch, the bank and the airspeed are changing continuously from start to finish; nothing is ever held constant. The ACS task is CA.V.D, and one complete lazy eight is the pair of 180 degree turns, one to each side.

concept: What the lazy eight demonstrates
q: What is the lazy eight actually testing?
a: Mastery of the airplane through a continuously changing flight condition. It tests smooth, coordinated control through constantly varying pitch, bank, airspeed and load factor, planning so that each milestone arrives at the right place, and the ability to divide attention between outside references and the airplane. The examiner is watching for symmetry: the two halves must be mirror images in pitch, bank, altitude and airspeed.

concept: ACS task code for the lazy eight
q: What is the ACS task code for the lazy eight?
a: CA.V.D, Task D in Area of Operation V, Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers, of the Commercial Pilot Airman Certification Standards FAA-S-ACS-7B. It sits between the chandelle, CA.V.C, and eights on pylons, CA.V.E.

concept: Entry configuration and airspeed for the lazy eight, Warrior II specific
q: What airspeed and configuration do you set before a lazy eight in the Warrior?
a: Clean, flaps up, trimmed and level, with power set for an airspeed at or below maneuvering speed. The 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II POH Section 2 gives design maneuvering speed as 111 KIAS at 2,440 lb, reducing to 88 KIAS at 1,531 lb, so I use that as the ceiling and interpolate for weight. That power setting is then left alone for the entire maneuver.

concept: Power is constant throughout the lazy eight
q: Do you change power during a lazy eight?
a: No. Power is set at the entry for an airspeed at or below maneuvering speed and stays constant for both halves; the airspeed changes come from trading altitude for speed and back again, not from the throttle. In the Warrior with its fixed-pitch propeller that means one throttle setting at the start, mixture rich, and hands off the throttle until the maneuver is finished.

concept: Minimum altitude for the lazy eight
q: What is the minimum altitude for a lazy eight?
a: The ACS requires an entry altitude that allows the maneuver to be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. The lazy eight returns to its entry altitude at each 180 degree point, so in practice I pick an entry altitude comfortably above that and verify it before each eight, allowing for the descending portions between the 90 and 180 degree points.

concept: Setting up the visual references for the lazy eight
q: How do you set up references for a lazy eight?
a: I pick a prominent point on the horizon 90 degrees off the entry heading, which is the point the nose will cross at the steepest-bank part of each half, and note reference features at roughly 45 and 135 degrees as well. The entry heading and its reciprocal are the 0 and 180 degree marks. Having real objects to aim at is what makes the milestones repeatable instead of guesswork.

q: Which way should the wind be before you start a lazy eight?
a: Perpendicular to the entry heading, so the first climbing turn is into the wind. The lazy eight has no ground-track standard, so wind does not affect the grading, but entering crosswind keeps the airplane from drifting away from the practice area and keeps the 90 degree horizon reference from sliding as the maneuver repeats.

concept: The entry to the 45 degree point of the first half
q: What is happening between the entry and the 45 degree point of a lazy eight?
a: A gradual climbing turn: the pitch is being raised continuously and the bank is being rolled in slowly, so that the airplane arrives at the 45 degree point with its highest pitch attitude and roughly 15 degrees of bank. The airspeed is decreasing and the altitude is increasing the whole way. The roll-in must be slow; the usual mistake is to get the bank in early and the pitch in late.

concept: The 45 degree point - bank, pitch, airspeed and altitude
q: What should bank, pitch, airspeed and altitude be at the 45 degree point?
a: Bank about 15 degrees and still increasing; pitch at its maximum nose-up for the whole maneuver; airspeed decreasing and roughly a third to halfway down from the entry speed toward the slowest speed of the maneuver; altitude climbing and roughly halfway to the apex. The ACS does not put a number on the 45 degree point, so it is graded on whether the pitch peaks there and whether the two halves match.

concept: The 45 to 90 degree segment of the lazy eight
q: What are you doing between the 45 and 90 degree points?
a: Letting the pitch come down toward the horizon while continuing to roll the bank in. The nose is still above the horizon so the airplane is still climbing, but more and more slowly, and the airspeed keeps falling. The whole segment is a single continuous blend of decreasing pitch with increasing bank, timed so that both arrive at their target values exactly at the 90 degree point.

concept: The 90 degree point - bank, pitch, airspeed and altitude
q: What should the airplane be doing exactly at the 90 degree point of a lazy eight?
a: Maximum bank of approximately 30 degrees, the slowest airspeed of the maneuver, the highest altitude of the maneuver, and the nose passing down through the horizon, so the pitch is momentarily level and the rate of climb momentarily zero. The 90 degree point is the apex of the loop; everything after it is a descending turn with the bank coming out.

concept: Where the airspeed is lowest in the lazy eight
q: Where is the airspeed lowest in a lazy eight and how slow should it get?
a: At the 90 degree point, where the airplane is at its apex with maximum bank. It should be the slowest speed of the maneuver but still comfortably above a stall with the wings at 30 degrees of bank; a stall warning at the apex means the pitch was too aggressive on the way up. The ACS does not name a speed for this point; it names only the entry airspeed plus or minus 10 knots at the 180 degree point.

concept: The 90 to 135 degree segment of the lazy eight
q: What is happening between the 90 and 135 degree points?
a: The nose is continuing down through and below the horizon while the bank is being rolled out, so the airplane is descending and accelerating. It is the mirror image of the 45 to 90 segment: decreasing bank with decreasing pitch. The descent and the roll-out are blended so that both reach their extremes together at the 135 degree point.

concept: The 135 degree point - bank, pitch, airspeed and altitude
q: What should bank, pitch, airspeed and altitude be at the 135 degree point?
a: Bank back down to about 15 degrees and still reducing, pitch at its lowest nose-down attitude of the maneuver, airspeed increasing back toward the entry speed, and altitude descending back toward the entry altitude. The 135 degree point mirrors the 45 degree point exactly, which is the test of whether the half is symmetrical.

concept: The 135 to 180 degree segment of the lazy eight
q: How do you fly from the 135 degree point to the 180 degree point?
a: Raise the nose back toward the horizon while taking out the last of the bank, so that the wings come level and the pitch reaches level flight attitude at the same instant the airplane passes through the reciprocal of the entry heading. The airspeed should be back to the entry speed and the altitude back to the entry altitude at that same moment. Everything has to arrive together; arriving level but off heading, or on heading but still descending, is the classic mis-timing.

concept: The 180 degree point - what the airplane must be doing
q: What is the required picture at the 180 degree point of a lazy eight?
a: Wings level, nose level, on the reciprocal of the entry heading within plus or minus 10 degrees, at the entry altitude within plus or minus 100 feet and the entry airspeed within plus or minus 10 knots. That instant is the only place in the maneuver the airplane is in level flight, and it is immediately the entry for the second half, flown in the opposite direction without a pause.

concept: The second half mirrors the first in the opposite direction
q: What happens after the 180 degree point of a lazy eight?
a: The second half begins immediately in the opposite direction, with no pause and no level segment: a climbing turn the other way, maximum pitch at its 45, maximum bank and minimum speed at its 90, lowest pitch at its 135, and level again at its 180, which puts the airplane back on the original entry heading, altitude and airspeed. The two halves together are one complete lazy eight, and they must be symmetrical.

concept: How many loops make one lazy eight
q: How many 180 degree turns make up one lazy eight?
a: Two, one in each direction, which together return the airplane to its original heading. The examiner will usually ask for a specified number of symmetrical loops, commonly two complete eights, and will be comparing them to each other as well as comparing the halves within each eight.

concept: The concept of constant change in the lazy eight
q: What does constant change mean in a lazy eight?
a: It means no parameter is ever steady: pitch, bank, airspeed, altitude, turn rate and control pressures are all changing continuously throughout, and there is no point where the airplane holds an attitude. The only exception is power, which is set once and not touched. Any flat spot, any moment where the bank or the pitch is parked while something else catches up, is the error the examiner is looking for.

concept: Why the examiner cares about constant change
q: Why does the examiner care that nothing is held constant in a lazy eight?
a: Because a maneuver with no steady state cannot be flown by chasing instruments or by memorizing a sight picture; it can only be flown by feel, planning and continuous coordination. That is exactly the skill a commercial certificate is meant to certify. If the pilot can hold symmetry through every combination of pitch, bank and airspeed the airplane can produce, the airplane is genuinely being flown rather than managed.

q: What is the altitude tolerance on a lazy eight and where is it applied?

q: What airspeed tolerance applies to a lazy eight?

q: What heading tolerance applies to the lazy eight?
a: Plus or minus 10 degrees at the 180 degree point, meaning the wings must come level within 10 degrees of the reciprocal of the entry heading. I establish it before the maneuver by setting the seat where it will be for the whole flight and noting, in a known bank, what part of the wing lines up with a ground point. concept: The pylon moves ahead of the reference line - diagnosis and correction
q: The pylon appears to move ahead of your reference line. What is wrong and what do you do?
a: I am above pivotal altitude, so I descend. Above pivotal altitude the airplane's turn rate is greater than the rate at which the bearing to the pylon is changing, so the airplane is turning faster than the pylon is going by and the pylon creeps forward toward the nose. Lowering the nose slightly reduces the altitude, and at the lower altitude the geometry matches again and the pylon stops moving. The correction is altitude, never rudder.

concept: The pylon moves behind the reference line - diagnosis and correction
q: The pylon appears to drift back toward the tail. What is wrong and what do you do?
a: I am below pivotal altitude, so I climb. Below pivotal altitude the airplane is not turning fast enough to keep up with the bearing change to the pylon, so the pylon falls back behind the reference line toward the tail. Raising the nose slightly climbs the airplane back to the pivotal altitude for the current groundspeed and the pylon stops moving aft. The correction is altitude, never rudder.

concept: The reference line phrasing, and how to keep the two cases straight
q: How do you keep straight which way to correct when the pylon moves?
a: I use one sentence: the pylon moves the way the airplane needs to not go. If the pylon moves forward, the airplane is high and must come down; if the pylon moves aft, the airplane is low and must climb. The Airplane Flying Handbook states it from the other side, in terms of the reference line moving relative to the pylon, which says the same thing inverted, so I always say which one I mean before answering.

concept: Never using rudder to hold the pylon
q: Why must you never use rudder to hold the pylon?
a: Because rudder only yaws the nose, which swings the reference line onto the pylon without correcting the altitude error that caused the problem, so the error is still there and it is now hidden. It also puts the airplane in a slip or a skid, and a skidding, steeply banked turn at low altitude with the pilot looking out of the side window is a classic stall and spin setup. The pylon is held with altitude and nothing else.

concept: Why bank varies around the circuit
q: Why does the bank angle change as you go around a pylon?
a: Because the airplane's path over the ground is not a circle. With a wind, the radius of turn for a given bank varies with the square of the groundspeed, so holding the wingtip line on the pylon produces a steeper bank on the downwind side, where the groundspeed and the radius are greatest, and a shallower bank on the upwind side. The bank is a result of the geometry, not something the pilot sets and holds.

concept: Where the altitude is highest and lowest in the circuit
q: Where in eights on pylons is your altitude highest and where is it lowest?
a: Highest where the groundspeed is highest, which is downwind, and lowest where the groundspeed is lowest, which is upwind, because pivotal altitude rises and falls with the square of the groundspeed. So the airplane is climbing as it turns from upwind to downwind and descending as it comes back around into the wind. That matches the page's note that a descent will likely be required heading back into the wind.

concept: Selecting the pylons
q: How do you choose the two pylons?
a: Two distinct, easily seen objects such as silos, isolated trees or road intersections, at the same elevation if possible, far enough apart that there is a short straight-and-level segment between them but close enough that the eight is continuous, on a line roughly perpendicular to the wind so the airplane crosses between them on a downwind diagonal, over sparsely populated ground with landing options within gliding distance.

q: What altitude limits apply to eights on pylons in practice?
a: Pivotal altitude at normal training groundspeeds works out roughly between 600 and 1,000 feet above the pylons, which sits right against the regulatory floor. Under 14 CFR 91.119 I must stay at least 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure over other than congested areas, and I must be able to make an emergency landing without undue hazard, so the pylons are chosen over open, sparsely populated terrain with fields available.

concept: Eights on pylons is not a constant radius or constant altitude maneuver
q: How are eights on pylons different from turns about a point?
a: Turns about a point is a constant altitude, constant radius maneuver where the bank is varied to hold the ground track. Eights on pylons has no radius requirement at all: the airplane's altitude is varied to hold a line of sight, the ground track is whatever the geometry produces, and the altitude changes continuously around the circuit. It is the only ground reference maneuver in which the pilot deliberately climbs and descends.

concept: Common error - selecting unsuitable pylons
q: What goes wrong when the pylons are badly chosen?
a: Pylons too close together leave no straight-and-level segment between them, so the airplane rolls from one steep bank straight into the other; too far apart and the eight becomes two separate turns with a long cruise between them. Pylons lined up with the wind rather than across it make the entry diagonal impossible to fly downwind. Pylons at different elevations give two different pivotal altitudes, which confuses the whole maneuver.

concept: Common error - not entering at the correct pivotal altitude
q: What is the effect of entering eights on pylons at the wrong altitude?
a: The pylon starts moving along the reference line immediately and the pilot spends the first circuit chasing it instead of flying the maneuver. The entry altitude should be the computed pivotal altitude for the downwind entry groundspeed plus the pylon elevation, so the airplane is close to correct when the first turn begins and only small corrections are needed. Entering at a guessed altitude is the most common reason the first eight is unsatisfactory.

concept: Common error - using rudder to hold the pylon
q: What is the most dangerous error in eights on pylons?
a: Yawing the airplane with rudder to drag the reference line back onto the pylon. It looks like it works, so pilots keep doing it, but it produces a skid at low altitude in a steep bank with the pilot's attention outside the cockpit, which is the classic stall and spin accident. It also hides the altitude error instead of correcting it, so the airplane drifts further from pivotal altitude.

q: Your bank keeps coming out at 45 degrees around the pylon. What is wrong?

The ACS limits the bank to 40 degrees, so the correction is to roll out a little earlier on the entry diagonal and fly the next turn at a greater distance from the pylon.

q: What happens if you do not enter on the downwind diagonal?
a: The maneuver starts out of phase with the wind, so the pivotal altitude is changing in the wrong direction relative to where the airplane is in the circuit, the two halves of the eight come out unequal, and the straight-and-level segment between the pylons does not line up. The entry is specifically a downwind 45 degree diagonal between the two pylons because that puts the highest pivotal altitude at the point where the maneuver begins.

concept: Common error - over-controlling and chasing the pylon with large altitude changes
q: What does over-controlling look like in eights on pylons?
a: Large pitch inputs producing climbs and descents that overshoot the pivotal altitude, so the pylon swings forward, then aft, then forward again and the airplane porpoises around the circuit. The required corrections are small and continuous: a slight change of pitch attitude, held long enough to see the pylon stop moving, rather than a pull or a push big enough to feel.

concept: Common error - loss of coordination in the turns
q: Why is coordination hard in eights on pylons and what is the standard?
a: Because the bank is changing continuously around the circuit, the pitch is being used for altitude, and the pilot's eyes are outside, so rudder pressures get forgotten. The ACS requires accurate, coordinated airplane control throughout, with the ball centered; the temptation is to let the airplane slip or skid because it momentarily puts the reference line where the pilot wants it, which is both a deviation and a hazard.

concept: What happens if the whole eight is flown at one fixed altitude
q: Could you fly the whole maneuver at one altitude in no wind?
a: In a genuine zero-wind condition, yes: with no wind the groundspeed is the same on every heading, so the pivotal altitude is constant and the airplane could hold one altitude all the way around both pylons. With any wind at all the groundspeed varies with heading and so does the pivotal altitude, which is why the real maneuver is a continuous shallow climb and descent, highest downwind and lowest upwind.
